Nymphas
NIM-fas
proper noun
A Greek name, a contracted form (as of Nymphodorus) bearing the element nymphe, “bride” or “nymph.”

Biblical Definition

Nymphas is a believer at or near Laodicea in whose house a congregation of the saints met, greeted by Paul in the close of Colossians: “Salute the brethren which are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the church which is in his house” (Col 4:15). Here we see the early church in its native form, gathered not in grand buildings but in the homes of its members, where a godly host opened his doors that the body of Christ might assemble for the Word, prayer, and the breaking of bread. Such house-churches dot the New Testament: that of Aquila and Priscilla (Rom 16:5), that in the house of Philemon (Phm 2), and this of Nymphas. To host the church was a costly and honourable service, exposing the household to expense and, in days of persecution, to danger. Nymphas stands therefore as a pattern of hospitality used for the gospel, of a Christian home set apart to the worship of God. Of the man himself we know nothing further. His house at Laodicea sat near a church the risen Christ would soon rebuke for lukewarmness (Rev 3:14–19), a sobering nearness. Yet Nymphas himself is named with honour, a saint whose dwelling became a sanctuary, and whose ordinary house was made holy by the assembling of the people of God within it.

Webster 1828 Definition

A believer of the Laodicean region in whose house a church assembled, greeted by Paul in Colossians.

expand to see more

NYMPHAS, a Christian near Laodicea who hosted a church in his house.

Greeted by Paul together with “the church which is in his house” (Col 4:15).

His Greek name is a contracted form bearing the element nymphe, “bride.”

His household exemplifies the New Testament pattern of house-churches.

He dwelt near Laodicea, the church later rebuked for lukewarmness (Rev 3:14–19).

Key Scripture

Col 4:15 — "Salute the brethren which are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the church which is in his house."

Rom 16:5 — "Likewise greet the church that is in their house. Salute my wellbeloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ."

Phm 1:2 — "And to our beloved Apphia, and Archippus our fellowsoldier, and to the church in thy house:"

Heb 13:2 — "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares."

Modern Corruption

The honourable service of hospitality, the Christian home opened for the worship of God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Nymphas is the dignity of the house-church and of hospitality spent upon the gospel. A man opened his home, and it became a place where Christ was worshipped and His people gathered.

Our age prizes private comfort and guards the home against intrusion; Nymphas teaches the opposite, a dwelling held loosely and offered freely to the saints. The church does not depend upon costly buildings but upon believing households and the assembling of the people of God. To host the church is no small thing, but a service the Lord honours and Scripture records.

Hebrew Roots

A Greek personal name compounded with nymphe, “bride,” here borne by a host of the church.

expand to see more

Nymphas — a contracted Greek name, as of Nymphodorus, “gift of the nymphs.”

The element nymphe means “bride” or “young woman.”

The same word names the Bride, the church, in the New Testament.

His name marks him a Gentile believer of Asia Minor.

Scripture preserves the name only in Colossians 4:15.

Usage

"The church which is in his house met under the roof of Nymphas."

"Like Nymphas, believers may open their homes for the worship of God."

"Paul greeted Nymphas as host of a congregation near Laodicea."
